Exponential growth can't keep going forever because the equation assumes nothing ever runs out. Real islands have a fixed amount of seed, a fixed amount of nesting space, and Daphne Major is only 0.34 km^2. Once there are lots of birds, each individual bird gets less food than before, so more of them starve and fewer of them successfully raise chicks. That means the per capita birth rate drops and the per capita death rate goes up, so r itself shrinks instead of staying at 0.17, and the curve bends over instead of shooting up.

K is about 1,200 birds. My evidence is the 1982-1990 rows. In logistic growth dN/dt = rN(K-N)/K, and the (K-N)/K part gets smaller and smaller as N approaches K, until it's basically 0 and the population stops changing. Growth is actually fastest in the middle, around N = K/2 = 600, which lines up with the 1972-1976 part of the table where it's gaining a couple hundred birds every two years.

The drought is density-independent. A drought is a weather event, it doesn't care how many finches are on the island. It would have dried up the seed crop the same amount whether there were 85 finches or 8,000, so the proportion of birds killed isn't set by the density of birds, it's set by the climate. (i) Food competition: as the population grows there are more birds eating from the same fixed seed supply. Per capita there is less food, so at high density more birds starve and the ones that survive are in worse condition and lay fewer eggs. At low density every bird can find plenty of seed. So the death rate rises as density rises, which is what density-dependent means. (ii) Disease: more birds means more disease. When the population is big, sickness spreads through it and can wipe out a lot of the birds at once. Diseases are worse in bigger populations.

(ii) Disease transmission is density-dependent because pathogens need contact to spread. Nitrogen starts as N2 gas in the air, which plants can't use because the triple bond is too strong. N(3) = 980 * e^(0.17*3)

So the population would go from 980 to roughly 1,632 birds in 3 years if it kept growing exponentially.
Exponential growth can't keep going forever because the exponential model assumes resources are unlimited and that nothing is holding the population back - no competition, no predators, no disease, unlimited seeds and nesting spots. That's not how a real island works. Daphne Major is only about 0.34 km^2 and there is only so much seed on it. As N gets bigger, each bird gets a smaller share of the seeds, so more birds starve and fewer of them can raise chicks. That means the per capita birth rate drops and/or the per capita death rate goes up, so r itself shrinks. Once r hits 0 the population stops growing, which is the carrying capacity. Basically the growth curve bends from a J shape into an S shape.

K is about 1,200 birds. The evidence is the last part of the table. From 1982 on the numbers are 1,180, 1,210, 1,195, 1,200, 1,205. That's eight years where the population isn't trending up or down anymore, it's just wobbling in a narrow band right around 1,200. Before that (1978-1982) the population was climbing fast, 380 to 820 to 1,180, and then it just stops climbing. A population that levels off and oscillates a little around one value is sitting at its carrying capacity, because the island can't support more than that. As the population gets close to K the growth rate slows down. In the logistic equation dN/dt = rN(K-N)/K, the (K-N)/K part is the thing that matters. When N is small, (K-N)/K is close to 1 so the population grows almost exponentially. When N gets near 1,200, K-N gets close to 0, so the whole term goes to about 0 and dN/dt goes to about 0 too. The fastest growth is at N = K/2, which here is about 600 birds, and looking at the table that's around 1972-1974 when the population jumped 480 to 750. So growth rate is highest in the middle and then falls off to nothing at K. Notice the growth rate slowing doesn't mean the population is shrinking, it just means it's adding fewer birds each year.

The 1977 drought is DENSITY-INDEPENDENT. Justification: the drought is a climate thing, it doesn't care how many finches are on the island. If there had been 100 finches or 10,000 finches, the rain still doesn't fall and the plants still don't make seeds, and roughly the same fraction of the birds die either way. The severity of the effect isn't set by the density of the population, it's set by an abiotic factor, so it's density-independent. (i) Food competition as density-dependent: Daphne Major produces a roughly fixed amount of seed in a normal year. When there are only 300 birds, each bird can find plenty of seeds, especially the easy small ones. As the population climbs toward 1,200, that same seed supply gets split more ways, so per capita food goes down. Birds then have to eat the big tough seeds they're bad at cracking, more of them starve, and females that are underweight lay fewer eggs. So the death rate rises and the birth rate falls specifically BECAUSE density went up - the strength of the effect depends on N, which is what density-dependent means. (ii) Disease transmission as density-dependent: when the population is dense the birds are packed closer together, feeding at the same seed patches and roosting near each other. A pathogen needs contact between an infected bird and a susceptible bird to spread, and the rate of those contacts goes up as density goes up (transmission is proportional to infected density times susceptible density). At low density an infected bird might die without ever passing it on, but at 1,200 birds on a tiny island an outbreak can rip through the whole flock. So a bigger proportion of the population gets sick and dies at high density than at low density, which limits the population more as it grows.
